title: Oncogenes vs. tumor suppressors
blurb: A stuck gas pedal vs. broken brakes, shown on KRAS and p53.

text.simple: Think of a cell like a car. **Oncogenes** are like a gas pedal stuck down. **Tumor suppressors** are like brakes. Cancer happens when the gas is stuck, the brakes are broken, or both.
text.student: **Oncogenes** (e.g. KRAS, MYC) drive growth when mutated to be overactive; one bad copy is often enough. **Tumor suppressor genes** (e.g. TP53, RB1) normally restrain growth; usually both copies must be lost. [@nci_genetics] [@weinberg]
text.deep: Oncogenes typically carry gain-of-function, often dominant, mutations at recurrent hotspots (e.g., KRAS G12). Tumor suppressors carry loss-of-function mutations distributed across the gene, often with loss of heterozygosity (Knudson's two-hit model). [@vogelstein2013]

text.simple: KRAS is a tiny switch. It flips **on** when a growth signal arrives, then flips itself **off**. Cancer mutations break the 'off' part, so it stays on.
text.student: KRAS is ON when holding GTP and OFF when holding GDP (shown here). Mutations like **G12** stop KRAS from switching itself off, so growth signals keep firing. [@waters2018]
text.deep: Oncogenic G12/G13/Q61 substitutions impair intrinsic and GAP-stimulated GTP hydrolysis, locking KRAS in the GTP-bound state that engages RAF and PI3K effectors. [@waters2018]

text.simple: p53 is the cell's emergency brake. When DNA is damaged, p53 grabs onto DNA and switches on genes that stop the cell, or tell it to self-destruct.
text.student: p53 is a **transcription factor**: it binds DNA (shown here) and turns on genes like **p21** that halt division. TP53 is the most commonly mutated gene in human cancer. [@vogelstein2013]
text.deep: Most TP53 mutations are missense changes in the DNA-binding domain shown here, abolishing sequence-specific transactivation of targets such as CDKN1A, MDM2 and BAX. [@vogelstein2013]

steps.title: See the brake work, in real data

note.simple: We turned off ATR, a DNA-damage alarm. In the healthy-like cell, look for **MDM2** and **FDXR** in the top genes. Those are genes p53 switches on. The cancer cell can't do this, because its p53 is broken.
note.student: Both results are ● measured. In RPE1 (working p53), ATR knockdown raises p53 target genes like **MDM2, FDXR and TP53I3**. In K562 (broken p53), these don't appear. Instead, heat-shock genes rise.
note.deep: RPE1 ATR knockdown induces a canonical p53 transcriptional program (MDM2, FDXR, TP53I3) and suppresses the mitotic program; K562 lacks this response, consistent with TP53 loss. Lineage differences may also contribute.

steps.title: Try it: lift the gas pedal

note.simple: Turning off KRAS barely changes K562! These leukemia cells don't run on KRAS. Their stuck pedal is BCR-ABL1 instead.
note.student: KRAS knockdown in K562 is measured and weak (not statistically clear). K562's growth is driven by BCR-ABL1, not KRAS. A cancer is only 'addicted' to its own driver genes.
note.deep: The weak KRAS phenotype in K562 illustrates oncogene addiction being driver-specific; KRAS-mutant pancreatic or lung lines would be expected to respond strongly. RPE1 is predicted (not in its screen).
